newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania still hopes to be in NATO's first round.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania still hopes to be in NATO's first round.

text.p: The Baltic state of Lithuania, anxious to defend its hard-won independence, still hopes to be in the first round of NATO expansion, according to President Algirdas Brazauskas.
Brazauskas told Reuters in an interview on Saturday that first round membership remains his nation's top priority in foreign policy despite Russian objections.
"We are very firm in pursuing our official line...Lithuania and other NATO aspirants have the right to get into the first round of NATO enlargement," Brazauskas said.
"We have not dropped this as our major foreign policy goal," he said.
"Lithuania's position is that all states that seek NATO membership should begin accession talks at the same time," he added.
Six years after quitting the Soviet Union, Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours Latvia and Estonia view the alliance's protective embrace as their only shield from a potentially hostile Russia.
Their bid for NATO membership will likely be on the agenda of this week's summit meeting between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and his American counterpart Bill Clinton.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are tipped to be the first countries invited to join the alliance at the Madrid summit in July.
Analysts and diplomats say that the Baltic countries have almost no chance of making the first round because Moscow would view such a move as a direct provocation.
Moscow has strong objections to NATO's enlargement plans and is particulary sensitive about the Baltics, the Soviet Union's western flank during the Cold War and home to large Russian minorities.
Lithuania and its Baltic neighbours are worried that they may be sacrificed on the altar of big power politics.
Bitter memories of Yalta, the 1945 conference in which Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt drew up the political map of post-War Europe, remain firmly entrenched in the Baltic mind.
Baltic aspirations for independence were quashed at Yalta and the countries' fear that another big power deal in Helsinki could leave them stranded.
"We do not want to be left out of NATO and left in a grey zone or in the sphere of influence of another state," Brazauskas said.
Despite his background as a former Communist party leader, Brazauskas has built himself a solid pro-reform and pro-NATO reputation.
"NATO enlargement should not be a painful process or a source of conflict," Brazauskas said.
He added that the alliance must clearly spell out its goals to the Kremlin. "I am convinced that NATO should legitimise its goals and make them clear to Russia," he said.
